translations.text: There was a man from Arimathea, in Zibah, in the hill country of Ephraim. His name was Elkanah, son of Jerahmeel, son of Eli, son of Tohu, from Nasib in Ephraim.
He had two wives. The name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no child.
Year after year, the man went up from his city, Arimathea, to worship and sacrifice to the Lord God of hosts at Shiloh. Eli and his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the Lord there.
One day Elkanah offered a sacrifice and gave portions to his wife Peninnah and to her sons and daughters.
He gave Hannah one portion, because she had no child. But Elkanah loved Hannah more than Peninnah, and the Lord had closed her womb.
For he did not give her a child in her distress and in the sorrow of her soul. She was saddened because the Lord had closed her womb, so that she could not have a child.
He did this year after year when she went up to the house of the Lord. She was saddened and wept and would not eat.

Her husband Elkanah said to her, “Hannah!” She said to him, “Here I am, my lord.” He said to her, “Why are you weeping? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart troubled? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”
Hannah rose after eating at Shiloh and stood before the Lord. Eli the priest was sitting on a chair beside the threshold of the Lord's temple.
In anguish of soul, she stood in prayer to the Lord and wept bitterly, saying:

“Lord, Lord God of hosts, if you will look upon the suffering of your servant and remember me, and give your servant a male child, I will give him as an offering before you until the day of his death. He shall drink neither wine nor intoxicating drink, and no iron blade shall touch his head.”
As she continued standing in prayer before the Lord, Eli the priest watched her mouth.
She was speaking in her heart. Her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard. The Lord heard her, but Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli's young servant said to her, “How long will you remain drunk? Rid yourself of your wine and go away from the Lord's presence.”
Hannah answered and said, “No, my lord. I am a woman whose spirit is troubled. I have drunk neither wine nor intoxicating drink, but I am pouring out my soul before the Lord.
Do not consider your servant a wicked woman, for I have been distraught until now because of my great sorrow and sadness.”
Eli answered her and said, “Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant you all the requests you have made of him.”
Hannah said, “Your servant has found favor in your sight.” The woman went on her way and entered her lodging. She ate with her husband and spoke, and her face was no longer sad.
They rose early in the morning, worshiped the Lord, and went on their way. Elkanah returned to his house in Arimathea and lay with his wife Hannah, and the Lord remembered her.
She conceived, and when her time came, she gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, saying, “Because I asked the Lord God of hosts for him.”
The man Elkanah and his entire household went up to offer the yearly sacrifice and his vows at Shiloh, and he brought all his tithes.
Hannah did not go up with him, for she said to her husband, “Not until this child goes up there, once I have weaned him, to appear before the Lord and remain there forever.”

Her husband Elkanah said to her, “Do whatever seems good in your eyes. Stay here until you have weaned him, and may the Lord establish what has come from your mouth.” So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him.

She went up with him to Shiloh with a three-year-old bull, [?], an ephah of fine flour, and a jar of wine. They entered the house of the Lord at Shiloh, with the child accompanying them, and presented him before the Lord.

His father slaughtered the sacrifice that he offered to the Lord year after year. He presented the child and slaughtered the bull for the child's redemption. Hannah, the child's mother, brought the child to Eli.
And she said, “[?], my lord, as you live, I am the woman who stood here before you, praying to the Lord.
For this child I prayed, and the Lord granted me the request I made of him.
And I lend him to the Lord for all the days that he lives; he will be lent to the Lord.” And they bowed down there before the Lord.
And Hannah prayed and said, “My heart is made firm in the Lord, and my horn is raised in my God. My mouth is opened wide against my enemies; I rejoice in your salvation.
For there is none holy like the Lord, and none righteous like our God, and none holy besides you.
Do not boast or speak arrogantly, and let no proud words come from your mouth, for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and God prepares his works.
The bows of the mighty have grown weak, and the weak have clothed themselves with strength.
Those who were full of bread have dwindled, and the hungry have settled in the land. For the barren woman has borne seven, and the woman who bore many children has dwindled in her children.
The Lord puts to death and brings to life; he brings down to the underworld and brings up.
The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and raises up.
He lifts the needy from the earth and raises the poor from the dung heaps, to seat them with the mighty of the people, and makes them inherit a throne of glory.
He grants the vows of the one who makes a vow, and has blessed the years of the righteous, for a mighty man does not become strong by his own strength.

The Lord weakens his adversaries; the Lord is holy. Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the mighty man boast in his strength, nor the rich man boast in his riches. Rather, let those who boast boast in this: understanding and knowing the Lord, and doing justice and righteousness in the midst of the earth. The Lord went up into heaven and thundered, and he himself, who is righteous, judges the ends of the earth. He gives strength to our kings and will raise the horn of his anointed one.”
And they left him there before the Lord and went to their home in Ramathaim. And the child Samuel served in the presence of the Lord before Eli the priest.
And the sons of Eli the priest were wicked sons and did not know the Lord.
And the priest’s entitlement from the people was this: whenever anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest’s servant would come while the meat was cooking, with a three-pronged meat fork in his hand.

He would thrust it into the basin, or into the large bronze cauldron, or into the pot, and the priest would take for himself everything that came up on the meat fork. This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to sacrifice at the house of the Lord in Shiloh.
And before the fat had been burned, the priest’s servant would come and say to the man offering the sacrifice, “Give the priest meat to roast; I will not take from you meat boiled in the pot.”

And the man offering the sacrifice would say, “Let the fat first be burned, as the law requires, and afterward take for yourself whatever you desire.” But he would say, “No, you must give it now; if you do not give it, I will take it by force.”
And these sins of the young men were very great before the Lord.
And the child Samuel ministered before the Lord, wearing an ephod.
And his mother would make him a little robe and bring it to him year after year, when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
And Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife and said, “May the Lord give you offspring from this wife in return for the one you lent to the Lord.” And the man went to his own place.
And the Lord visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three more sons and three daughters. And the child Samuel grew up before the Lord.
And Eli was very old, and he heard everything his sons were doing to the Israelites, and how they slept with the women who had made vows at the entrance of the tent of testimony.
And he said to them, “Why do you do these things that I hear about from the mouths of all the Lord’s people?
No, my sons! The report I hear is not good, for it keeps God’s people from serving him.

For if a man sins against another man, people will stand in prayer for him before the Lord. But if he sins against the Lord, who will stand in prayer for him?” But they did not listen to their father’s voice, because the Lord was determined to destroy them.
And the boy Samuel continued to grow and was pleasing to God and to people.

And an angel of God came to Eli and said, “Thus says the Lord: I plainly revealed myself to the whole household of your father while they were in the land of the Egyptians, servants of Pharaoh’s household.

I chose your father’s house from all the tribes of Israel to serve me as priests, to approach my altar, to offer incense, and to wear the ephod before me. I gave your father’s house all the offerings made by fire by the Israelites for food.
Why did you look upon my incense and my sacrifices with a shameless eye, and honor your sons more than me, blessing the produce of all Israel’s sacrifices that are before me?

Therefore, thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: I said that your household and your father’s household would walk before me forever. But now the Lord says: Far be it from me! Instead, I will honor those who honor me, and whoever despises me will be dishonored.
Look, days are coming when I will destroy your offspring and the offspring of your father’s household, and there will be no old man in your household.
You will continually look with sorrow upon all the good that the Lord, the God of Israel, will do, and there will never be an old man in your house.
Yet I will not destroy every man belonging to you from my altar, so that his eyes may weep and his life waste away. And all who remain in your household will fall by the sword of men.
And this will be the sign for you that will come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: both will die on the same day.
I will raise up for myself a faithful priest who will do everything that is in my heart and in my soul. I will build him a lasting house, and he will walk before my anointed one all his days.

And everyone who remains in your household will come to bow down before him for a small silver coin and a loaf of bread, and will say, ‘Assign me to some position in your priesthood so that I may eat bread.’”
And the boy Samuel served the Lord before Eli the priest. The word of the Lord was precious in those days, and there was no vision giving revelation.
And it happened that on that day Eli was sleeping in his place. His eyes had begun to grow dim, and he could not see.
The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was sleeping in the Lord’s temple, where the ark of God was.
And the Lord called and said, “Samuel, Samuel!” And he said, “Here I am.”
And he ran to Eli and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” And he said, “I did not call you. Go back and sleep.” And he went back and slept.
The Lord called again and said, “Samuel, Samuel!” Samuel got up and went to Eli a second time and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” He said, “I did not call you, my son. Go back and sleep.”
And Samuel was previously acquainted with God, but the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him.
And the Lord called Samuel again, for the third time. He got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” And Eli understood that the Lord was calling the boy.
And Eli said to Samuel, “Go back and sleep, my son. If he calls you, say, ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant will listen.’” And Samuel went and slept in his place.
And the Lord came, stood over him, and called him as he had the first and second times: “Samuel, Samuel!” And Samuel said, “Speak, Lord, for your servant will listen.”
And the Lord said to Samuel, “Look, I am carrying out my words in Israel, so that both ears of everyone who hears them will ring.
On that day I will bring upon Eli everything I have spoken against his household. I will begin it and bring it to completion,
just as I told him that I would exact vengeance from his household forever because of his sons’ lawlessness. For his sons blasphemed God, and he did not discipline them.
And not only that, but I swore to Eli’s household that the lawlessness of Eli’s household would never be atoned for by incense or sacrifices.”
Samuel slept until morning, rose early in the morning, and opened the doors of the house of the Lord. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
Eli said to Samuel, “Samuel, my son.” He answered, “Here I am.”
He said, “What did he say to you? Do not hide it from me. May God do such and such to you, and more besides, if you hide from me a single word of everything he said in your hearing.”
Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. Eli said, “He is the Lord. Let him do whatever is good in his sight.”
Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and not one of his words fell to the ground.
All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was trustworthy as a prophet of the Lord.

The Lord continued to reveal himself at Shiloh, for the Lord appeared to Samuel at Shiloh according to the word of the Lord. Samuel was established as a trustworthy prophet of the Lord throughout all Israel, from one end of the land to the other. Eli was very old, and his sons continued in their ways, and their way was evil.
In those days the Philistines gathered against Israel. Israel went out to fight them and camped at Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek.
The Philistines drew up their battle lines against Israel, and battle was joined. The men of Israel were defeated before the Philistines, and four thousand men were struck down there in battle.

The army returned to the camp, and the elders of Israel said, “Why has the Lord defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of our God here from Shiloh, so that it may come into our midst and save us from the hands of our enemies.”

The people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, who sits enthroned upon the cherubim. Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, went with the ark of the covenant of God.
When the ark of the covenant of the Lord came into the camp, all Israel shouted loudly, and the earth resounded.
The Philistines heard the sound of the shouting and said, “What is the sound of that great shout in the camp of the Hebrews?” Then they learned that the ark of the Lord had come into the camp.
The Philistines were afraid and said, “Those gods of theirs have come into the camp! Save us today, Lord! Woe to us, for nothing like this happened to us yesterday or the day before!
Woe to us! Who will save us from the hands of those mighty gods? These are the gods who struck Egypt with every plague and throughout the wilderness.
Be strong and be men, Philistines, lest you become slaves to the Hebrews as they were slaves to you. Be men and fight them!”
They fought them, and the men of Israel fled, each to his own tent. The slaughter was very great, and thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.
The ark of God was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
A Benjaminite ran from the camp and came to Shiloh that same day, with his clothes torn and earth on his head.
When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his chair by the gate, watching the road, for his heart was troubled about the ark of God. The man entered the city to report the bad news, and the city cried out.
Eli heard the sound of the outcry and said, “What is the sound of that outcry?” The man hurried in to report the bad news to Eli.
Eli was ninety-eight years old. His eyes had failed, and he could not see. Eli said to the men standing around him, “What is the sound of that outcry?”
The man hurried in to Eli and said to him, “I am the one who came from the camp, and I fled from the battle today.” He said, “What has happened, my son? Tell me.”

The young man answered, “The men of Israel fled before the Philistines, and the people suffered very heavy losses. Both your sons, Hophni and Phinehas, have died, and the ark of God has been captured.”
When he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his seat beside the gate. His neck broke, and he died, for he was an old and heavy man. He had judged Israel for twenty years.

His daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and close to giving birth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband had died, she wept and gave birth, for her labor pains came upon her.
As she was dying, the women standing around her said to her, “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son.” But she gave no answer, and her heart took no notice.
They named the child Ichabod because of the ark of God, her father-in-law, and her husband.
They said, “The glory of Israel has departed,” because the ark of the Lord had been captured and because her mother-in-law and her husband had died.
The Philistines took the ark of God and brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
The Philistines took the ark of the Lord, brought it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside Dagon.

The people of Ashdod rose early the next morning and entered the temple of Dagon. They saw Dagon fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the Lord. They raised Dagon and set him back in his place. The hand of the Lord weighed heavily upon the people of Ashdod. He tormented them and struck them in their buttocks, both Ashdod and its surrounding territory.

When they rose early the next morning, there was Dagon, lying face down on the ground before the ark of the covenant of the Lord. Dagon’s head and both his feet were broken off and scattered on the ground, and both his hands had fallen onto the threshold. Only Dagon’s torso remained.
For this reason, neither the priests of Dagon nor anyone entering Dagon’s temple in Ashdod steps on the threshold of Dagon’s temple to this day. Instead, they step over it and pass through.
The hand of the Lord weighed heavily upon Ashdod. He struck them in their buttocks and caused mice to swarm in their fields, and there was great deadly panic in the city.
When the men of Ashdod saw what was happening, they said, “The ark of God must not remain with us, for his hand weighs heavily upon us and upon Dagon our god.”

They sent and gathered all the rulers of the Philistines to them and said, “What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” The people of Gath said, “Let the ark of the God of Israel be moved to us.” So the ark of God was moved to Gath.

After it was moved there, the hand of the Lord came upon the city, and there was very great turmoil. He tormented the men of the city, from the least to the greatest, and struck them in their buttocks. The people of Gath made seats for themselves.

They sent the ark of God to Ashkelon. When the ark of God entered Ashkelon, the people of Ashkelon raised an outcry and said, “Why have you brought the ark of the God of Israel around to us, to kill us and our people?”

They sent and gathered all the rulers of the Philistines and said, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its own place, so that it does not destroy us and our people.” For a deadly panic had spread throughout the whole city, becoming very severe ever since the ark of the God of Israel entered there.
Those who were still alive and had not died were struck in their buttocks, and the city’s cry rose to heaven.
The ark of the Lord was in the territory of the Philistines for seven months, and mice swarmed in their land.
The Philistines called their priests, diviners, and wise men and said, “What shall we do with the ark of the Lord? Tell us what we should send with it when we return it to its place.”

They said, “If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, the Lord’s covenant, do not send it away empty. You must give him an offering as reparation for the plagues. Then you will be healed, and he will be reconciled with you; otherwise his hand may not withdraw from you.”

They said, “What shall we give as reparation for his punishment?” They said, “Make five golden buttocks and five golden mice, corresponding to the number of the rulers of the Philistines, for the plagues are upon you, your rulers, and your people.”
“Now make images of your buttocks and likenesses of the mice that are destroying the land, and give glory to the Lord, so that he may lighten his hand upon you, your gods, and your land.”
“Why do you harden your hearts, as Egypt and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? When he made a mockery of them, did they not release the people, and did they not depart?”
“Now take and make a new cart, and take two cows that have calved for the first time, without their calves. Yoke the cows to the cart, and take their calves away from them, back home.”

“Take the ark of the Lord and place it on the cart. Put the golden objects that you are giving him as reparation for his punishment in a sack [?] beside it. Send it away and set it moving, and let it go.”

“Watch: if it goes into its own territory by way of Beth-shemesh, then he has brought these great calamities upon us. But if not, we will know that it was not his hand that came upon us, but that something happened to us by chance.”
The Philistines did so. They took two cows that had calved for the first time and yoked them to the cart, and they shut their calves inside.
They placed the ark of the Lord on the cart, along with the sack [?], the golden mice, and the images of their buttocks.

The cows went straight along the road leading to Beth-shemesh. They followed a single path, toiling along, and did not turn aside to the right or to the left. The rulers of the Philistines followed it as far as the borders of Beth-shemesh.
The people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valleys. They raised their eyes and saw the ark of the Lord, and they rejoiced as it approached.
The cart entered the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh, and they stopped there. Nearby was a large stone. They split the wood of the cart and offered the cows as burnt offerings to the Lord.

The Levites took down the ark of the Lord and the sack [?] beside it, with the golden objects inside, and placed them on the large stone. The men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices to the Lord that day.
The five rulers of the Philistines watched and returned to Ekron that day.
These were the golden buttocks that the Philistines gave to the Lord as reparation for his punishment: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron.

The golden mice corresponded to the number of all the Philistine cities belonging to the five rulers, from the fortified cities to the villages of the Perizzite, as far as the stone on which they placed the ark of the Lord’s covenant, which is in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh to this day.

The sons of Jeconiah were not pleased with the men of Beth-shemesh because they had seen the ark of the Lord. He struck down fifty thousand and seventy men among them, and the people mourned because the Lord had struck the people with very great blows.
The men of Beth-shemesh said, “Who can walk before this holy Lord God? And now, to whom shall the ark of the Lord go up from us?”
They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim and said, “The Philistines have returned the ark of the Lord. Come down and take it up to yourselves.”

And the men of Kiriath-jearim came and brought up the ark of the covenant of the Lord from there. They took it to the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill, and consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the covenant of the Lord.
And from the day when the ark came to be in Kiriath-jearim, many days passed, amounting to twenty years, and the whole house of Israel looked to the Lord.

And Samuel spoke to the whole house of Israel and said, “If you have returned to the Lord with all your heart, remove the foreign gods and the sacred groves from among you. Set your hearts toward the Lord and serve him alone, and he will deliver you from the hands of the Philistines.”
The Israelites put away the Baals and the sacred groves of Ashtoreth and served him alone.
And Samuel said, “Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the Lord for you.”

And they gathered at Mizpah and drew water, and he poured it out on the ground before the Lord. They fasted that day and said, “We have sinned before the Lord.” And Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah.
And the Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, and the rulers of the Philistines went up against Israel. The Israelites heard of it and were afraid of the Philistines.
And the Israelites said to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to the Lord your God for us, so that he may deliver us from the hands of the Philistines.”
And Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a burnt offering to the Lord, together with all the people. Samuel cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him.

And while Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines approached to fight against Israel. The Lord thundered with a mighty sound against the Philistines that day, and they were thrown into confusion and fell before Israel.
And the men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, striking them down as far as the place below Beth-car.
And Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and old Beth-shan. He named it Ebenezer, “Stone of Help,” and said, “Up to this place the Lord has helped us.”
And the Lord humbled the Philistines, and they no longer came up against the borders of Israel. The hand of the Lord was against the Philistines throughout all the days of Samuel.

And the Philistines returned the cities they had taken from the Israelites and gave them back to Israel, from Ashkelon to Gath. They rescued the territories of Israel from the hands of the Philistines, and there was peace between Israel and the Amorites.
And Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.
He went year by year, making a circuit through Bethel, Gilead, and Mizpah, and judged Israel at all those holy places.
He would return to Ramathaim, for his house was there. There he judged Israel, and there he built an altar to the Lord.
And when Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
And these are the names of his sons: the firstborn was Joel, and the name of the second was Abijah. They were judges in Beersheba.
And his sons did not walk in his ways, but turned aside to pursue dishonest gain. They took bribes and perverted justice.
All the men of Israel gathered and came to Samuel at Ramathaim.
And they said to him, “Look, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint a king over us to judge us, like the other nations.”
And the statement displeased Samuel, because they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” And Samuel prayed to the Lord.
The Lord said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of this people in what they have said to you, for it is not you they have rejected; they have rejected me from reigning over them.”
“According to all the deeds they have done against me, from the day I brought them out of Egypt until today, forsaking me and serving foreign gods, so they are doing to you as well.”
“Now listen to their voice, but solemnly warn them and tell them the rights of the king who will reign over them.”
And Samuel spoke all the words of the Lord to the people who had asked him for a king.
And he said, “These will be the rights of the king who reigns over you: he will take your sons and make them his charioteers, horsemen, and runners before his chariots.
He will appoint them as his commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, and set them to reap his harvest, gather his produce, and make his weapons and equipment for his chariots.
He will take your daughters to be ointment makers, cooks, and bakers.
He will take the best of your fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his servants.
He will take a tenth of your crops and vineyards and give it to his eunuchs and servants.
He will take your male servants, your female servants, your best cattle, and your donkeys, and levy a tenth for his own work.
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you will become his servants.
On that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you chose for yourselves, but the Lord will not listen to you in those days, because you yourselves chose a king for yourselves.”
But the people were unwilling to listen to Samuel and said to him, “No! Rather, a king shall reign over us,
so that we too may be like the other nations. Our king will judge us, go out before us, and fight our battles.”
Samuel heard all the words of the people and repeated them in the Lord’s hearing.
The Lord said to Samuel, “Listen to their voice and appoint a king to reign over them.” And Samuel said to the men of Israel, “Let each of you go to his own town.”
There was a man from the descendants of Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Ared, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, son of a Benjaminite. He was a powerful man.
He had a son named Saul, a fine, well-built man. Among the Israelites there was no man better than he. He stood a head taller than all the people.
The donkeys belonging to Saul’s father were lost. Kish said to his son Saul, “Take one of the servants with you, get up, and go look for the donkeys.”

They went and passed through the hill country of Ephraim and through the land of Sarisa, but did not find them. They passed through the land of Shaalim, but they were nowhere to be found. They passed through the land of the Benjaminites, but did not find them.
When they came to Siph, Saul said to his young servant who was with him, “Come, let us go back, lest our father stop thinking about the donkeys and begin worrying about us.”

The young man said to him, “Look, there is a man of God in this town, a highly respected man. Everything he says certainly comes true. Now let us go there, so that he may tell us which way to go, and we will go.”
Saul said to the young man who was with him, “Suppose we go—what shall we bring the man of God? Even the bread in our bags has run out, and we have nothing else with us to bring the man of God.”
The young man answered Saul again and said, “Look, I have a quarter of a shekel of silver in my hand. You can give it to the man of God, and he will tell us which way to go.”
Formerly in Israel, whenever someone went to inquire of God, he would say, “Come, let us go to the seer,” for the people formerly called a prophet a seer.
Saul said to his young servant, “What you say is good. Come, let us go.” And they went to the town where the man of God was.
As they were going up the slope toward the town, they met girls coming out to draw water and said to them, “Is there a seer here?”
The girls answered them, “There is. Look, he is just ahead of you. Hurry now, for he has come to the town for this day, because the people have a sacrifice today at Bamah.”

When you enter the city, you will find him there before he goes to Bamah to eat, for the people do not eat until he arrives, because he blesses the sacrifice, and afterward the invited guests eat. Now go up, for you will find him there today.
They went up to the city, and as they entered the middle of the city, Samuel came out toward them on his way to Bamah.
The Lord had revealed this to Samuel one day before Saul came to him:

“Tomorrow at this same hour I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin. You shall anoint him ruler over my people Israel, and he will save my people from the hands of the Philistines. For I have seen the suffering of my people, and their cry has reached me.”
Samuel saw Saul, and the Lord said to him, “Here is the man of whom I told you, ‘He will rule over my people.’”
Saul approached Samuel in the middle of the city and said, “Tell me, which is the seer’s house?”
Samuel answered Saul, “I myself am the seer. Go up ahead of me to Bamah, and you will eat with me today. Tomorrow I will send you on your way, and I will tell you everything that is in your heart.
As for the donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found. And to whom do the finest things in Israel belong, if not to you and all your father’s household?”
Saul answered, “Am I not descended from a Benjaminite, from a small tribe of Israel, and from the smallest clan in all the territory of Benjamin? Why have you spoken to me in this way?”
Samuel took Saul and his young servant and brought them to his lodging. He gave them a place above the invited guests, who numbered about thirty men.
Samuel said to the cook, “Give me the portion that I gave you and told you to keep with you.”

The cook cooked the thigh and the saddle attached to it and placed it before Saul. Samuel said to Saul, “Here is the remaining portion. Put it before you and eat, so that it may be a testimony to you from the people, and you shall chew it.” Saul ate with Samuel that day.
He went down from Bamah into the city, and they spread bedding for Saul on the roof, and he slept.
At dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof and said, “Get up and come, and I will send you on your way.” Saul got up, and he and Samuel went outside.
As they were going down to the edge of the city, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell your young servant to go ahead of us.” He went ahead. “But you must stand here today and hear the words of the Lord.”

Samuel took the flask of oil, poured it on Saul’s head, kissed him, and said to him, “Has not the Lord anointed you ruler over his inheritance and over his people Israel? You will rule over the Lord’s people and save them from the hands of their enemies all around. This will be a sign to you that the Lord has anointed you:

When you leave me today, you will find two men by Rachel’s tomb on the mountain of Benjamin, running vigorously. They will say to you, ‘The donkeys you went to look for have been found. Your father has stopped concerning himself with the donkeys and is worried about you, saying, “What shall I do about my son?”’

You will go farther from there and reach the oak of Deborah. There you will find three men going up to God at Bethel: one carrying three young goats, one carrying three containers of bread, and one carrying a skin of wine.
They will ask about your well-being and give you two loaves of bread, and you shall accept them from their hands.

Then you shall go to the hill of God, where the Philistine garrison is. When you enter the town, you will meet a band of prophets coming down from Bamah, with a flute, a tambourine, a trumpet, and a lyre before them, and they themselves prophesying.
The Spirit of the Lord will come upon you, and you too will prophesy with them and be changed into another man.
When these signs come upon you, do whatever your hand finds to do, for God is with you.
You shall go down to Gilgal ahead of me, and I will come down to you to offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. Wait seven days, until I come to you and tell you what you shall do.
When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God changed his heart into another heart, and all these signs came to pass for him that day.
He came from there to the hill, and there was a band of prophets coming to meet him. The Spirit of God came upon him, and he prophesied among them.

When all those who had known him previously saw that he too was prophesying among the prophets, the people said to one another, “What is this that has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
One of them answered and said, “Who is his father, if not Kish?” Therefore it became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
He finished prophesying and came to the hill.
His relative said to him and his servant, “Where did you go?” They said, “To look for the donkeys. When we saw that they were nowhere to be found, we went to Samuel.”
His relative said to Saul, “Tell me what Samuel said to you.”
Saul said to his relative, “He told me plainly that the donkeys had been found.” But he did not reveal to him what Samuel had said to him about the kingship.
Samuel gathered all the people before the Lord at Mizpah.

He said to the Israelites, “Thus the Lord, the God of Israel, has spoken, saying: ‘I am the one who brought the Israelites out of Egypt and rescued you from the hands of Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, and from all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’

“But today you have rejected God, who saves you from all those who surround you and oppress you, and you have said, ‘No, instead appoint a king over us.’ Now stand before the Lord according to your divisions, your tribes, and your thousands.”
Samuel brought forward all the tribes of Israel, and the lot fell to the tribe of Benjamin.

He brought forward the tribe of Benjamin by its clans, and the lot fell to the clan of Matri. They brought forward the clan of Matri man by man, and the lot fell to Saul son of Kish. He looked for him but could not find him.
Samuel asked the Lord again, “Will the man come here?” The Lord said, “Look, he is hiding among the baggage.”
He ran and brought him from there and stood him among the people. He was taller than all the people by a shoulder’s height.
Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the one whom the Lord has chosen for himself? There is no one like him among all of you.” All the people understood and said, “Long live the king!”
Samuel told the people the rights of the king, wrote them in a book, and placed it before the Lord. Samuel dismissed all the people, and each went to his own place.
Saul went to his home in Gibeah, and valiant men whose hearts the Lord had stirred went with Saul.
But wicked men said, “Who is this man, that he should save us?” They despised him and brought him no gifts.
After a month had passed, Nahash the Ammonite came up and encamped against Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to Nahash the Ammonite, “Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.”
And Nahash the Ammonite said to them, “I will make a covenant with you on this condition: that you gouge out every one of your right eyes, and I will bring disgrace upon all Israel.”
And the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Give us seven days, and we will send messengers throughout all the territory of Israel. If there is no one to save us, we will come out to you.”
And the messengers came to Saul at Gibeah and spoke these words in the hearing of the people. And the people raised their voices and wept.
And behold, Saul was coming from the field in the morning, and Saul said, “What is the matter, that the people are weeping?” And they told him the message of the people of Jabesh.
And the Spirit of the Lord stirred upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger burned fiercely.

And he took two oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel by the messengers, saying, “Whoever does not come out after Saul and Samuel, this is what will be done to his oxen.” And the fear of the Lord fell upon all the people of Israel, and they rallied as one man.
And he mustered them at Bezek. All the men of Israel who came out numbered six hundred thousand, and the men of Judah seventy thousand.

And he said to the messengers who had come, “Say this to the men of Jabesh-gilead: ‘Tomorrow, when the sun grows hot, you will have deliverance.’” And the messengers came to the city and told the men of Jabesh, and they rejoiced.
And the men of Jabesh said to Nahash the Ammonite, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do to us whatever pleases you.”

And the next day Saul divided the people into three companies. They entered the camp during the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the sun grew hot. Those who remained were scattered, and no two of them were left together.
And the people said to Samuel, “Who was it who said, ‘Saul must not reign over us’? Hand those men over, and we will kill them.”
And Samuel said, “No one shall be put to death on this day, for today the Lord has brought deliverance to Israel.”
And Samuel spoke to the people and said, “Let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingdom.”

And all the people went to Gilgal, and there Samuel anointed Saul as king before the Lord at Gilgal. And there they offered sacrifices of peace offerings before the Lord, and Samuel and all the people rejoiced greatly there.
Samuel said to all the men of Israel, “Look, I have listened to your voice in everything you said to me, and I have appointed a king to reign over you.”
“And now, behold, the king goes before you. I am old; I will go and sit down. And behold, my sons are among you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day.”

Here I stand. Testify about me before the Lord and before his anointed one. Whose ox have I taken, or whose donkey have I driven away? Have I oppressed any of you, or deprived anyone of anything? From whose hands have I taken payment or sandals? Testify about me, and I will repay you.
And they said to Samuel, “You have not wronged us, deprived us, or oppressed us, and you have taken nothing from anyone’s hand.”

And Samuel said to the people, “Let the Lord be a witness among you, and let his anointed one be a witness this very day, that you have found nothing in my hand.” And they said, “Let him be a witness.”
And Samuel spoke to the people and said, “Let the Lord be a witness, who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought our fathers out of Egypt.”
Now come forward, and I will plead the case against you before the Lord and recount to you all the righteous deeds that the Lord has done among you and among your fathers.

“When Jacob and his sons entered Egypt, Egypt oppressed them. And our fathers cried out to the Lord, and the Lord sent Moses and Aaron and brought our fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place.”
“And they forgot the Lord their God, and he handed them over to Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin king of Hazor, and to the Philistines, and to the king of Moab, who fought against them.”
“And they cried out to the Lord and said, ‘We have sinned, for we have forsaken the Lord and served the Baals and the groves. Now rescue us from the hands of our enemies, and we will serve you.’”
And the Lord sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samson, and rescued you from the hands of your enemies all around, and you lived in safety.
And you saw that Nahash the Ammonite came against you, and you said, “No! Rather, let a king reign over us,” although the Lord our God was our king.
And now, here is the king whom you chose and whom you requested. See, the Lord has given you a king.

If you fear the Lord and serve him and listen to his voice and do not rebel against the command of the Lord, and if both you and the king who reigns over you follow the Lord, the hand of the Lord will not be against you or against your king.
But if you do not listen to the voice of the Lord and rebel against the command of the Lord, the hand of the Lord will be against you and against your king.
And now, stand and see this great thing that the Lord will do before your eyes.

Is it not the wheat harvest today? I will call upon the Lord, and he will send thunder and rain, and you will know and see that the evil you have done before the Lord by asking for a king for yourselves is great.
And Samuel called upon the Lord, and the Lord sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people greatly feared the Lord and Samuel.
And all the people said to Samuel, “Pray to the Lord your God for your servants, so that we do not die, for we have added to all our sins and evil deeds by asking for a king for ourselves.”
And Samuel said to the people, “Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil, but do not turn away from the Lord, and serve the Lord with all your heart.
And do not follow worthless things that neither benefit nor save, for they are not gods.
For the Lord will not reject his people for the sake of his great name, because the Lord graciously took you as his people.
And as for me, far be it from me to sin against the Lord by neglecting to pray for you. Serve the Lord, and I will show you the good and upright way.
Only fear the Lord and serve him faithfully with all your heart, for you have seen the great things he has done for us.
But if you act treacherously, both you and your king will perish.”
Saul was one year old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel for two years.

And Saul chose for himself three thousand men from the men of Israel. Two thousand were with him at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and one thousand were with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin. He sent the rest of the people away, each to his own home.
And Jonathan struck Nasib the Philistine, who was on the hill, and the Philistines heard about it. And Saul sounded the trumpet throughout the whole land and said, “The servants have shown contempt.”
And all Israel heard it said that Saul had struck Nasib the Philistine and that Israel had put the Philistines to shame. And the people rallied with a shout behind Saul at Gilgal.

And the Philistines had gathered for battle against Israel, and they came up against Israel with thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and people as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They came up and camped at Michmash, opposite Beth-horon to the south.
And the men of Israel saw that they were in distress as the enemy approached them, and the people hid in caves, stalls, rocks, ravines, and wells.
And those who were going to cross the Jordan crossed into the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people slipped away from him.
And he waited seven days according to the testimony, as Samuel had said, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and his people scattered away from him.
Saul said, “Bring the offerings so that I may offer burnt offerings and peace offerings.” And he offered the burnt offerings.
When he had finished offering the burnt offerings, Samuel came, and Saul went out to meet him and greet him.

Samuel said, “What have you done?” Saul said, “I saw that my people were scattering away from me, and you had not come as you had pledged for the appointed days, and the Philistines had gathered at Michmash.”
I said, ‘Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not entreated the Lord’s favor.’ So I forced myself and offered the burnt offerings.
Samuel said to Saul, “This is in vain for you, because you have not kept my commandment, which the Lord commanded. For the Lord would now have established your kingdom over Israel forever.
But now your kingdom shall not stand. The Lord will seek for himself a man after his own heart and appoint him ruler over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded you.”

Samuel arose and went on his way from Gilgal. The remaining people went up after Saul to meet the fighting men. When they arrived from Gilgal at Gibeah of Benjamin, Saul counted the people who were with him, about six hundred men.
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the people who were with them stayed at Gibeah of Benjamin, while the Philistines were encamped at Michmash.
The raiding force went out from the Philistine camp in three companies. One company headed along the road to Ophrah, toward the spring of Sogol.
And one company went along the road toward Beth-horon, and one company along the road toward Geba, extending toward the valley of Saba in the wilderness.
No ironworker could be found anywhere in the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, “Otherwise the Hebrews might make swords and spears.”
All the Israelites went down to the land of the Philistines, each to sharpen his scythe, his tool, his axe, and his sickle.
The crops were ready for reaping, and the charge for the implements was three shekels for a plowshare, with the same price for an axe and a sickle.
And during the fighting at Michmash, no sword or spear was found in the hands of any of the people who were with Saul and his son Jonathan, but they were found with Saul and his son Jonathan.
And he went out to the Philistines’ camp beyond Michmash, but he did not disclose it to his father.
One day Jonathan, Saul’s son, said to the young man who carried his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the Philistines’ ravines on the other side.” But he did not tell his father.
Saul was sitting at the top of the hill, beneath the pomegranate tree at Migdol, and about six hundred men from the people were with him.
And Ahijah, son of Ahitub, the brother of Cabiel, son of Phinehas, son of Levi, the priest of God at Shiloh, was wearing the ephod. The people did not know that Jonathan had gone.

Within the pass through which Jonathan sought to cross to the Philistine camp, among the ravines, there was a rocky crag on this side and a rocky crag on that side. The name of one was Bozez, and the name of the other was Seneh.
One crag was on the north, facing Michmash, and the other crag was on the south, facing Geba.

Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the ravines of those uncircumcised men. Perhaps the Lord will do something for us, for nothing prevents the Lord from saving through many or through few.”
His armor-bearer said to him, “Do whatever your heart desires. Here I am with you; my heart is like your heart.”
Jonathan said, “Look, we will cross over to the men and go toward them on our hands and knees.
If they say to us, ‘Stand back there until we tell you something,’ we will stay where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say, ‘Come up to us,’ we will go up, because the Lord has delivered them into our hands. This will be the sign for us.”
Both of them entered the Philistines’ ravines, and the Philistines said, “Look, the Hebrews are coming out of their holes where they have been hiding.”

The men in the ravines called out to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, saying, “Come up to us, and we will tell you something.” Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, “Come after me, for the Lord has delivered them into Israel’s hands.”
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and knees, and his armor-bearer went with him. They turned to face Jonathan, and he struck them down, while his armor-bearer kept striking behind him.
The first casualties that Jonathan and his armor-bearer inflicted were about twenty men, with arrows and hand-thrown stones in the field.
Panic broke out in the field, in the camp, and among all the people who were in the ravines. The raiders were terrified and would not exert themselves. The earth shook, and terror came from the Lord.
Saul’s watchmen in Gibeah of Benjamin saw that the camp was in turmoil, moving this way and that.
Saul said to the people who were with him, “Take a roll call and see who has gone away from us.” They took a roll call, and Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not found.
Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ephod.” For he carried the ephod, because the ark of God was before Israel that day.
While Saul was speaking with the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp kept growing louder. Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand.”
Saul and all the people with him went out and came to the battle. There each man’s sword was turned against his companion, and there was tremendous confusion.
The servants who had been with the Philistines yesterday and the day before, and who had gone up with their camp, turned back to join Israel, Saul, and Jonathan.
When all the Israelites who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines had fled, they too gathered and pursued them into battle.
The Lord saved Israel that day, and the battle spread around Beth-aven.

All the people with Saul numbered about ten thousand men, and the battle had spread through all the towns in the hill country of Ephraim. Saul acted foolishly that day. He put the people under a curse, saying, “Cursed be the man who eats food before evening, before I have taken vengeance on my enemies.” So none of the people ate any food.
Everyone in the land was eating, and there was a woodland full of bees opposite the field.
The army entered the apiary and passed through grumbling. No one brought his hand to his mouth, because the people feared the oath to the Lord.

Jonathan had not heard that his father had put the people under oath. He stretched out the tip of the staff in his hand, dipped it into a honeycomb, and brought his hand to his mouth. His eyes brightened.
Someone from the army spoke up and said, “Your father solemnly put the people under oath, saying, ‘Cursed be the man who eats food before evening.’” And the people grew faint.
When Jonathan learned this, he said, “My father has ruined the land. For my eyes can see again because I tasted a little of this honey.
If the people had eaten freely today from the spoil they found from their enemies, they would have inflicted great losses on the Philistines.”
That day he struck down the Philistines at Michmash, and the people became very weary.
The people rushed upon the spoil. They took flocks, herds, and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and ate them with the blood.
Saul was informed, “The people have sinned against the Lord, because they have eaten with the blood.” Saul said, “You have acted lawlessly at Geththama. Roll a large stone here to me.”

Saul said, “Spread out among the people and tell them to bring here each his own ox and each his own sheep. Slaughter them on this stone and eat them. Do not sin against the Lord by eating with the blood.” That night each of the people brought what he had with him, and they slaughtered them there.
Saul built an altar to the Lord there. That was the first altar Saul began to build to the Lord.

Saul said, “Let us go down after the Philistines tonight and plunder them until daybreak, and let us not leave a single man alive.” They said to him, “Do whatever seems good to you.” The priest said, “Let us draw near to God here.”
Saul asked God, “Shall we go down after the Philistines? Will you deliver them into Israel’s hands?” But the Lord did not answer him that day.
Saul said, “Bring all the tribes of Israel here, and find out and see who is responsible for these sins today.
For as the Lord who saved Israel lives, even if the answer points to Jonathan my son, he shall surely die.” But no one among all the people answered.
He said to all the men of Israel, “You shall be on one side, and Jonathan my son and I shall be on the other.” The people said to Saul, “Do whatever seems good to you.”

Saul said, “Lord, God of Israel, why have you not answered your servant today? If the wrongdoing today is in me or in Jonathan my son, give a revelation; but if the injustice is in your people Israel, give atonement.” They cast lots, and Jonathan and Saul were selected, while the people were excluded.

Saul said, “Cast lots between me and Jonathan my son, and whoever the Lord selects by the lot shall die.” The people said to Saul, “Let this not happen.” But Saul compelled the people, and they cast lots between him and Jonathan his son, and the lot fell on Jonathan.
Saul said to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done.” Jonathan told him, saying, “I tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff in my hand, and now I am to die.”
Saul said to him, “May God do this to me, and more besides, if you do not surely die today.”

The people said to Saul, “Far be it that the man who brought this great deliverance to Israel should die today! As the Lord lives, not a hair of his head shall fall to the ground, for the people of God committed these sins.” The people stood in prayer before the Lord for Jonathan that day, and he did not die.
Saul turned back from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own places.

Saul came to reign and was appointed over Israel. He waged war against all his enemies on every side: against Moab, the Ammonites, the Edomites, Bethor, the king of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he brought deliverance.
He performed great deeds of strength, struck down Amalek, and rescued Israel from the hands of those who oppressed them.
Saul’s sons were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. The names of his two daughters were Merab, the firstborn, and Michal, the second.
His wife’s name was Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz, and the name of his army commander was Abner, son of Ner, the son of a relative of Saul.
Kish, Saul’s father, and Ner, Abner’s father, were sons of Jamin, son of Abiel. Thirty-eight.
There was fierce warfare against the Philistines throughout Saul’s days. Whenever Saul saw any strong man or any valiant warrior, he gathered them to himself.
Samuel said to Saul, “The Lord sent me to anoint you as king over his people Israel. Now listen to the words of the Lord.
This is what the Lord of hosts says: ‘Now I will exact vengeance for what Amalek did to Israel, how he confronted them on the road when they came up from Egypt.’

And now go and strike Amalek and Harim and everything that belongs to him. Do not spare any of them, but destroy him and wipe them out, from man to woman, from child to nursing infant, from ox to sheep, and from camel to donkey.
And Saul gave orders to the people and mustered them at Alim: four hundred thousand soldiers and thirty thousand soldiers of Judah.
And Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in ambush in the ravine.

And Saul said to the Kenite, “Go, flee from among the Amalekites, so that I do not destroy you with them, for you showed kindness to all the children of Israel when they came out of Egypt.” And the Kenite withdrew from among Amalek.
And Saul struck Amalek from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt.
And he captured Agag, the king of Amalek, alive, and they slaughtered the whole people of Harim with the edge of the sword.

And Saul and all the people spared Agag alive, along with the best of the sheep, the herds, the provisions, the vineyards, and all the good things, and he was unwilling to destroy them. But they destroyed everything that was worthless and despised.
And the word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying:
“I regret that I made Saul king, because he has turned away from me and has not kept my words.” And Samuel was distressed, and Samuel cried out to the Lord all night.

And Samuel rose early and went to meet Israel in the morning. And Samuel was informed, “Saul came to Carmel and erected a monument for himself, then turned his chariots around and went down to Gilgal.”

And Samuel came to Saul, and there he was offering burnt offerings to the Lord, the first of the spoil that he had brought from Amalek. And Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, “Blessed are you by the Lord! I have carried out what the Lord said.”
And Samuel said, “Then what is this sound of sheep in my ears, and the sound of oxen that I hear?”
And Saul said, “I brought these from Amalek. The people spared the best of the sheep and oxen to sacrifice to the Lord your God, and I destroyed the rest.”
And Samuel said to Saul, “Listen, and I will tell you what the Lord said to me this night.” And he said to him, “Speak.”
And Samuel said to Saul, “Are you not small in his sight, commander of the scepter of the tribe of Israel? And the Lord anointed you king over Israel.
And the Lord sent you on a journey and said to you, ‘Go and destroy Amalek, who has sinned against me, and wage war against them until you have put an end to them.’
Why, then, did you not obey the voice of the Lord, but rushed to seize the spoil and did evil in the sight of the Lord?”
And Saul said to Samuel, “Because I listened to the voice of the people, and I went on the journey on which the Lord sent me, and I brought Agag, the king of Amalek, and destroyed Amalek.
And the people took sheep and cattle from the spoil, the best of what was marked for destruction, to sacrifice before the Lord God at Gilgal.”

And Samuel said, “Are burnt offerings and sacrifices as pleasing to the Lord as obedience to the voice of the Lord? Look, obedience is better than a choice sacrifice, and submission than the fat of rams.
For divination is sin, and your household idol brings suffering and hardship. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord will reject you from being king over Israel.”
And Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, for I transgressed the word of the Lord and your word, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.
And now forgive my sin and return with me, and I will bow down before the Lord your God.”
Samuel said to Saul, “I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord will reject you as king over Israel.”
Samuel turned to leave, and Saul seized the hem of his cloak and tore it.
Samuel said to him, “Today the Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hands and will give it to a neighbor of yours who is better than you.
Israel will be divided in two, and the Lord will not turn back or change his mind, for he is not like a man, changing his mind when he himself makes a threat.”
And Saul said, “I have sinned. But honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me so that I may worship the Lord your God.”
Samuel returned after Saul, and Saul bowed down before the Lord.
Samuel said, “Bring me Agag, king of Amalek.” Agag approached him trembling, and Agag said, “Is death so bitter?”
Samuel said to Agag, “As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women.” And Samuel killed Agag before the Lord at Gilgal.
Samuel went to Ramathaim, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah.
Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, for Samuel mourned over Saul. And the Lord regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.

The Lord said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn over Saul, when I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and come. I will send you to Jesse in Bethlehem, for I have seen among his sons a king to reign for me.”
Samuel said, “How can I go? Saul will hear about it and kill me.” The Lord said, “Take a heifer from the herd for me, and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the Lord.’
Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what to do. You shall anoint the one I tell you.”
And Samuel did everything the Lord had told him and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city trembled when they met him and said, “Do you come in peace, seer?”
He said, “It is peace. I have come to sacrifice to the Lord. Purify yourselves and rejoice with me today.” He purified Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they came in, he saw Eliab and said, “Surely the Lord’s anointed is here before him.”

The Lord said to Samuel, “Do not look at his appearance or his great height, because I have rejected him. God does not see as a human being sees: a human being looks at the face, but God looks at the heart.”
Jesse called Abinadab, and he passed before Samuel. Samuel said, “The Lord has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse made Shammah pass before him, and Samuel said, “The Lord has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse made his seven sons pass before Samuel, and Samuel said to Jesse, “The Lord has not chosen any of these.”

Samuel said to Jesse, “Are these all your sons?” He said, “There is still the youngest, and he is tending the flock.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send and bring him, for we will not sit down until he comes here.”
He sent and brought him. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and pleasing in appearance to the Lord. The Lord said to Samuel, “Rise and anoint David, for this one is good.”
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him among his brothers. The Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day onward. Samuel rose and went to Ramathaim.
The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord tormented him.
His servants said to him, “Look, an evil spirit from the Lord is tormenting you.

Let your servants speak before you and seek for our lord a man who knows how to play the lyre. When the evil spirit from God comes upon you, he will play the lyre, and you will feel relief, and he will soothe you.”
Saul said to his servants, “Find me a man who plays well, and bring him to me.”

One of his young men answered and said, “I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite who knows how to perform psalms. He is a wise man, a warrior, intelligent and eloquent, handsome in appearance, and the Lord is with him.”
Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, “Send me your son David, who is with your flock.”
Jesse took a measure of bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sent them to Saul by his son David.
David came to Saul and stood before him in his service. Saul loved him greatly, and he became his quiver-bearer.
Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, “Let David remain before me, for he has found favor in my eyes.”
Whenever the evil spirit came upon Saul, David took the harp and played it with his hand. He soothed Saul, who felt relief, and the evil spirit departed from him.
The Philistines gathered their armies for battle and assembled at Socoh in Judah. They camped between Socoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel gathered in the valley and drew up their battle line against the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on the mountain on one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side, with the valley between them.
A mighty man came out from the Philistine battle line. His name was Goliath, from Gath, and his height was six cubits and a span.
He had a helmet on his head and wore a coat of armor. His armor weighed five thousand shekels of bronze and iron.
He had bronze greaves on his thighs and a bronze shield on his back.
The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, and its point weighed six hundred shekels of iron. His armor-bearer walked before him.

He came forward, stood, and called out to Israel’s battle line, saying to them, “Why have you come out to draw up your battle line against us? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not Hebrews, servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me.
If he can fight me and strike me down, we will become your servants. But if I defeat him and strike him down, you will become our servants and serve us.”
The Philistine said, “Today I have defied Israel’s battle line. Give me a man, and let the two of us fight in single combat.”
When Saul and all Israel heard the Philistine’s words, they were struck with terror and were greatly afraid.
There was a man who was the son of an Ephrathite man from Bethlehem in Judah named Jesse. Jesse had eight sons, and in Saul’s days the man was old, advanced among men.
Jesse’s three eldest sons had followed Saul to the war. The names of his sons who went to the war were Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab his second, and Shammah his third.
David was the youngest, and the three eldest had followed Saul.
David went back from Saul to tend his father’s sheep in Bethlehem.
The Philistine came forward morning and evening and took his stand for forty days.
Jesse said to his son David, “Take this measure of roasted grain meal and these ten loaves for your brothers. Hurry to the camp and give them to your brothers.
Take these ten cheeses to the commander of a thousand. See how your brothers are doing, and find out whether they need anything.”
Saul and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of the Oak, fighting against the Philistines.

David rose early in the morning, left the sheep with the herdsmen, picked up his things, and went as Jesse had commanded him. He came to the plain, to the army that was going out to the battle line, and they raised a battle cry.
And the Israelites and the Philistines drew up their battle lines opposite one another, line facing line.
David left his belongings in the care of the keeper, ran to the battle line, and came and asked his brothers how they were.
While he was speaking, the Jaminite, a man named Goliath, a Philistine from Gath, came out from the foreigners’ battle lines and spoke the same words as before. David heard him.
When all the Israelites saw the man, they fled from him and were greatly terrified.

An Israelite said, “Do you see that man coming out? He comes out to taunt Israel. Whoever kills him, the king will make very wealthy, give him his daughter in marriage, and make his father’s household exempt from obligations in Israel.”

David spoke to the men standing around him and said, “What will be done for the man who strikes down that foreigner and removes the disgrace from Israel? For who is that uncircumcised foreigner to taunt the battle lines of the living God?”
And the people spoke to him in the same words, saying, “This is what will be done for the man who kills him.”

When his eldest brother Eliab heard him speaking to the men, Eliab became furious with David and said, “Why have you come down here at all? In whose care have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your arrogance and the wickedness of your heart. You came down to watch the battle.”
David said, “What have I done now? Surely these are only words?”
And he turned away from him toward another and spoke in the same words, and the people answered him as they had before.
The words David spoke were heard and reported to Saul, and he brought David to him.
David said to Saul, “Do not let my lord lose heart because of him. Your servant will go and fight that foreigner.”
Saul said to David, “You may not be able to go and fight the foreigner, for you are a boy, and he has been a warrior since his youth.”
David said to Saul, “Your servant used to tend his father’s sheep, and whenever a lion or a bear came and took a sheep from the flock,
I would go after it, strike it, and snatch the sheep from its mouth. If it rose against me, I would seize it by the throat, strike it, and kill it.

Your servant killed both the lion and the bear, and the uncircumcised foreigner will be like one of them. Shall I not now go, kill him, and remove the disgrace from Israel today? For who is that uncircumcised man who has taunted the armies of the living God?”

David said, “The Lord God, who rescued me from the lion’s grasp and the bear’s grasp, will also rescue me from the grasp of that uncircumcised foreigner.” Saul said, “Go, and may the Lord be with you.”
And Saul dressed David in his own garments, put a bronze helmet on his head, and clothed him in a coat of armor.
David strapped his sword over his armor and stumbled once and twice as he walked. David said to Saul, “I cannot walk with these, because I am not used to them.” They took the armor off him.

He took his staff in his hand, chose five smooth stones from the streambed, and put them in the shepherd’s bag in which he usually collected stones. With his sling in his hand, he approached the foreigner.
The foreigner kept coming closer to David, with his shield-bearer ahead of him.
When the foreigner looked and saw David, he despised him, because he was a youth, blond and with beautiful eyes.
The foreigner said to David, “What? Am I a dog, that you come against me with a staff and stones?” David said, “Indeed, you are even worse than a dog.” The foreigner cursed David by his gods.
The foreigner said to David, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and the wild beasts of the earth.”

David said to the Philistine, “You come against me with a sword, a spear, and a shield, but I come against you in the name of the Lord of hosts, the Lord of Israel’s armies, whom you have insulted today.

Today the Lord will hand you over to me, and I will kill you and take your head from you. Today I will give your corpse and the corpses of the Philistine army to the birds of the sky and the wild animals of the earth. Then the whole earth will know that there is a God in Israel,
and this whole assembly will know that the Lord does not save by sword or spear, for the battle belongs to the Lord, and the Lord will hand you over to us.”
The Philistine rose, came forward, and approached David, and David hurried and ran toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.
David put his hand into his bag, took a stone from it, and slung it, striking the Philistine on the forehead. The stone went through the helmet into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground.
David overpowered the Philistine with the sling and the stone. He struck the Philistine and killed him, though he had no sword in his hand.
David ran and stood over him, took his sword, drew it from its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.
The men of Israel and Judah rose, shouted, and pursued them as far as the entrance to Gath and the gates of Ekron. The wounded Philistines fell along the road as far as the gates of Gath and Ekron.
And the men of Israel returned from pursuing the Philistines and overran their camps.
David took the Philistine’s head and brought it to Jerusalem, and he put his weapons in his own tent.
When Saul saw David going out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, “Whose son is that young man, Abner?” Abner said, “As surely as you live, O king, I do not know.”
The king said, “Ask whose son the young man is.”
When David returned from striking down the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul, with the Philistine’s head in his hand.
Saul said to him, “Whose son are you, young man?” David said, “The son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem.”
When he finished speaking with Saul, Jonathan’s soul was bound to David’s soul, and Jonathan loved him as himself.
Saul took him into his service that day and did not let him return to his father’s house.
Jonathan made a covenant with him because he loved him as himself.
Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his armor, even his sword, his bow, and his belt.
David went wherever Saul sent him and acted wisely. Saul put him in command of the fighting men, and he was pleasing in the eyes of all the people and also in the eyes of Saul’s servants.

As they came in, when David returned from killing the Philistine, women dancers came out from all the towns of Israel to meet David, singing and dancing to meet King Saul, with tambourines, rejoicing, and cymbals.
The women sang in turn as they danced, saying, “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.”
Saul was displeased at these words and said, “They have given David tens of thousands, but they have given me thousands. Now what does he lack except the kingdom?”
Saul looked with suspicion from that day onward.
The next day an evil spirit from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied inside his house. David played music with his hand, as he did every day, and the spear was in Saul’s hand.
And he said, “I will strike David and pin him to the wall with this spear.” Saul hurled it, and David escaped from him twice.
Saul was afraid of David, because the Lord was with him but had departed from Saul.
Saul removed him from his presence and appointed him commander of a thousand, and he went out and came in at the head of the people.
And David acted wisely in all his ways, and the Lord was with him.
When Saul saw how wisely he acted, he was greatly afraid of him.
All Israel and Judah loved David, because he went out and came in at the head of the people.

Saul said to David, “Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you as your wife. Only be a valiant warrior for me and fight the Lord’s battles.” For Saul said, “Let my hand not be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him.”
David said to Saul, “Who am I, and what is the standing of my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the king’s son-in-law?”
When the time came to give Saul’s daughter Merab to David, she was given as a wife to Adriel the Meholathite.
Saul’s daughter Michal loved David. Saul was told, and the news pleased him.

Saul said, “I will give her to him as a wife, and she will become a snare to him.” And the hand of the Philistines was against Saul. Saul said to David, “Through these two you will become my son-in-law today.”
And Saul instructed his servants, saying, “Speak privately to David and say, ‘Look, the king is pleased with you, and all his men love you. Now become the king’s son-in-law.’”
Saul’s servants spoke all these words in David’s hearing. David said, “Does becoming the king’s son-in-law seem a small thing to you? I am a poor man of no distinction.”
Saul’s servants reported to him these words that David had spoken.

Saul said, “Say this to David: ‘The king wants no bride-price except a hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on the king’s enemies.’” Saul was planning to make him fall into the hands of the Philistines.
Saul’s servants told David these words, and David was pleased to become the king’s son-in-law. The allotted days had not yet elapsed.

David rose and went with his men and killed a hundred Philistine men. He brought their foreskins and presented the full number before the king, and he became the king’s son-in-law. Saul gave him his daughter Michal as his wife.
Saul saw and knew that the Lord was with him and that all Israel loved him.
He became still more afraid of David, and Saul remained hostile to David all his days.
The Philistine commanders went out, and on the many occasions when they went out, David acted more wisely than all Saul’s servants. His name was greatly honored.
Saul spoke to his son Jonathan and to all his servants about killing David.
Saul’s son Jonathan was very fond of David. Jonathan told David, “My father is seeking to kill you. Be on your guard tomorrow morning; hide yourself and stay in a hiding place.”
“And I will go out and stand beside my father in the open, where you will be, and I will speak to my father about you. I will see what happens and tell you.”
Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul and said to him, “Let the king not sin against his servant David, for he has not sinned against you, and his deeds have been very beneficial to you.

He took his life in his hands and struck down the Philistine, and the Lord brought about a great deliverance. All Israel saw it and rejoiced. Why would you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause?”
Saul listened to Jonathan and swore, saying, “As the Lord lives, he shall not die.”
Jonathan called David and told him all these things. Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence as he had been before.
War broke out again, and David grew strong in fighting the Philistines. He struck them very heavily, and they fled before him.
And this evil came upon Saul from the Lord. He was sitting in his house with his spear in his hand, and David was playing music with his hands.
Saul tried to drive the spear through David and into the wall, but David dodged away from Saul, and Saul drove the spear into the wall. David went out, departed, and escaped.

That night Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him so that he could kill him in the morning. Michal, David’s wife, told him, saying, “If you do not save your life tonight, you will be dead tomorrow.”
Michal lowered David through the window, and he fled, went away, and escaped.
And Michal took the household idols and placed them on the bed. She put a goat’s liver and a ball of hair at the head of the bed and covered it with a garment.
Saul sent messengers to seize David, and they said, “He is sick.”
He sent for David again and said, “Bring him to me in his bed, and I will kill him.”
The messengers came, and there were the ornamental coverings on the bed, with a goat’s liver and a ball of hair at the head of the bed.
And Saul said to Michal, “Why have you deceived me like this and let my enemy go, so that he escaped?” And Michal said to Saul, “He himself said, ‘Let me go, or I will kill you.’”
David fled and escaped, and came to Samuel at Ramathaim. He told him everything Saul had done to him. Samuel and David went and stayed at Naioth in Ramah.
