Saul was informed, and they said, “David is at Naioth in Ramah.”
Saul sent messengers to seize David. They saw the assembly of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing over them. The Spirit of God came upon Saul’s messengers, and they too prophesied.
Saul was told, and Saul sent other messengers, but they too prophesied. Saul again sent other messengers, and they too prophesied.
Saul became furious and went himself to Ramathaim. He came as far as the great well at Secu and asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” They said, “At Naioth in Ramah.”
He went from there to Naioth in Ramah, and the Spirit of God came upon him. He continued on his way, prophesying until he reached Naioth in Ramah.
He himself stripped off his clothes and prophesied before them. He fell down naked and remained so all that day and all that night. That is why they said, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
And David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came and spoke before Jonathan, saying, “What have I done? What is my offense, and what sin have I committed against your father, that he seeks my life?”
Jonathan said to him, “Far be it from you! You will not die. My father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. Why would my father hide this matter from me? It is not so.”

David answered Jonathan, “Your father knows very well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he says, ‘Jonathan must not know, in case he objects.’ But as the Lord lives and as you live, as I said, the matter between me and your father is settled, even to death.”
Jonathan said to David, “What do you desire? I will do it for you.”
David said to Jonathan, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and I will certainly not sit down to eat with the king. Let me go, and I will hide here in the field until the evening of the third day.
If your father notices my absence, say, ‘David earnestly asked my permission to go to Bethlehem, his city, because the whole clan has its annual sacrifice there.’
If he says, ‘Good,’ your servant will be safe. But if he answers harshly, know that he has resolved to do evil.

Show kindness to your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant with you before the Lord. If your servant is guilty of anything, kill me yourself. Why should you bring me to your father?”
Jonathan said, “Far be it from you! If I knew for certain that my father had decided to bring harm upon you, would I not tell you even in your own city?”
David said to Jonathan, “Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?”
Jonathan said to David, “Go and stay in the field.” And the two of them went into the field.

Jonathan said to David, “The Lord, the God of Israel, knows that I will question my father three times. Whether there is anything favorable toward David or anything bad, I will send word to you in the fields.

May the Lord do this and more to Jonathan if I do not discover the harm intended for you, tell you privately, and send you away so that you may go in peace. May the Lord be with you as he was with my father.
While I am still alive, show kindness to me; and if I die,
“And never withdraw your kindness from my household, not even when the Lord wipes out every one of David’s enemies from the face of the earth.”
let Jonathan’s name be found in David’s house. May the Lord demand an accounting from David’s enemies.”
Jonathan again made David swear because of his love for him, for he loved his dear friend’s life.
Jonathan said to him, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your empty seat will be noticed.
You will stay away for three days and be missed. Then come to the place where you hid on the working day, and sit beside that Ergab [?].
I will shoot three arrows as in hunting and send them toward the target.
I will send the boy and say, ‘Go, find the arrow.’ If I tell the boy, ‘The arrow is on this side of you; bring it here,’ then come, for you are safe and there is nothing wrong, as the Lord lives.
But if I tell the boy, ‘The arrow is beyond you,’ then go, for the Lord has sent you away.
As for the words that you and I have spoken, let the Lord be a witness between me and you forever.”
David hid in the field. The new moon came, and the king entered the chamber to eat.
The king sat in his usual seat, the seat by the wall. Jonathan arrived, and Abner sat beside Saul, but David’s place was empty.
Saul said nothing that day, for he thought, “Something must have happened to make him unclean, and he has not been purified.”
On the next day, the second day of the new moon, David’s place was empty. Saul said to his son Jonathan, “Why has Jesse’s son not come to the table either yesterday or today?”
Jonathan answered Saul, “He asked my permission to go to Bethlehem, his own town.

He said, ‘Let me go, for our clan has a sacrifice in the town, and my brothers have summoned me. Now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me go and see my brothers.’ That is why he has not come to the king’s table.”
Saul became angry with Jonathan and said to him, “You son of a traitorous girl! Do I not know that you are allied with Jesse’s son, to your own shame and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness?
For as long as Jesse’s son is alive, your kingdom will not be established. Now send and seize the young man, for he deserves to die.”
Jonathan answered his father Saul and said to him, “Why should he die? What has he done?”
Saul raised his spear against Jonathan to kill him. Jonathan knew that his father had decided to kill David.
Jonathan left the table in anger and fury. He ate no food on the second day of the month, for he was deeply distressed over David, because his father had made his decision concerning him.
In the morning Jonathan went out into the field, as he had arranged with David, as a testimony, and a little boy was with him.
He said to the boy, “Run and find the arrow that I shoot.” The boy ran, and he shot the arrow, and the boy brought it back.
The boy went to the place where Jonathan had shot the arrow, and Jonathan called after the boy, saying, “The arrow is farther beyond you!”
Jonathan called after the boy, saying, “Hurry! Be quick and do not stop!” Jonathan’s boy gathered the arrows and brought them to his master.
The boy knew nothing about it; only Jonathan and David knew the matter.
Jonathan gave his equipment to the boy and said to him, “Go into the city.”
The boy went in, and David rose from Argab, fell face down on the ground, and bowed to him three times. They kissed one another and wept over one another until they were utterly spent.
Jonathan said to David, “Go in peace. As we both swore in the Lord’s name and said, ‘May the Lord be a witness between me and you, and between my descendants and your descendants forever.’”
David rose and went away, and Jonathan entered the city.
David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech was alarmed when he met him and said to him, “Why are you alone, with no one accompanying you?”

David said to Ahimelech the priest, “The king has ordered me to carry out a task today. He said to me, ‘Let no one know about the matter for which I sent you and about which I gave you instructions.’ I instructed the young men to go to the place called ‘God’s Faithfulness, Phelmoni Elmoni.’”
“Now, if you have five loaves of bread at hand, give them to me for my needs, or whatever you can find.”
The priest of God answered David, saying, “I have no ordinary bread at hand, only holy bread. If the young men have kept themselves from women, they may eat it.”

David answered the priest and said to him, “We have kept ourselves apart from women since yesterday and the day before. When I set out on this journey, the young men were also purified. Although this journey itself is unclean, today it will be made holy by this act of mine.”

Ahimelech the priest gave him some of the bread set out before the Lord, because there was no bread there except the bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the Lord so that fresh, warm bread could be set before him on the day it was taken away.
One of Saul’s servants was there that day, detained [?] before the Lord. His name was Doeg the Syrian, and he tended Saul’s mules.
David said to Ahimelech, “Do you have a spear or a sword here at hand? I did not bring my sword or my equipment with me, because the king’s business pressed me to hurry.”

The priest said, “Here is the sword of Goliath, the foreigner, the Philistine whom you killed in the Valley of Elah. It is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want to take it with you, take it, because there is no other here.” David said, “There is none like it. Give it to me.” And he gave it to him.
David rose and fled from Saul that day, and David came to Achish, king of Gath.

The servants of Achish said to him, “Is this not David, the king of the land? Was it not about him that the dancers sang, saying, ‘Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”
And David took these words to heart and was greatly afraid of Achish, king of Gath.
He changed his expression before them and pretended to be mad that day. He danced at the city gates, let his saliva run down his beard, and played [?].
Achish said to his servants, “Look, you see that this man is possessed. Why are you bringing him to me?”
“Am I short of possessed men, that you bring this man to act possessed before me? Do not let him enter my house!”
David left there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. His brothers and his father's entire household heard about it and went down to him there.
And everyone in distress, everyone in debt, and everyone bitter in spirit gathered around him. He became their commander, and about four hundred men were with him.
David went from there to Mizpah in Moab and said to the king of Moab, “Let my father and mother stay with you until I know what God will do for me.”
He pleaded with the king of Moab, and they stayed with him the whole time that David was in the cave.
The prophet Gad said to David, “Do not stay in this cave. Get up and go to the land of Judah.” David left and settled in the city of Careth.
Saul heard that David and the men with him had been discovered. Saul was sitting on the hill, below the cultivated field at Ramah, with his spear in his hand, and all his servants stood around him.

Saul spoke to his servants who stood around him and said, “Listen, men of Benjamin! Will the son of Jesse really give all of you fields and vineyards? Will he make all of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds?

For all of you have conspired against me. No one told me when my son made a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you felt any concern for me or told me that my son had stirred up my servant against me as an enemy, as he is today.”
Doeg the Syrian, who was in charge of Saul’s mules, answered and said, “I saw the son of Jesse come to Nob, to the priest Ahimelech son of Ahitub.”
“He inquired of the Lord for him, gave him provisions, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
The king sent for Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all the sons of his father, the priests who were in Nob. They all came to the king.
And Saul said, “Listen, son of Ahitub.” And he said, “Here I am. Speak, my lord.”
Saul said to him, “Why have you and the son of Jesse conspired against me, giving him bread and a sword and inquiring of God for him, making him my enemy, as he is today?”
Ahimelech answered the king, “Who among all your servants is as faithful as David? He is the king's son-in-law, is in charge of all your orders, and is honored in your house.

Was it only today that I began to inquire of God for him? Certainly not! Let the king never lay such a charge against his servant or against my father's household, for your servant knows nothing at all about this matter, great or small.”
King Saul said, “You shall surely die, Ahimelech—you and your father's entire household.”

The king said to the guards standing around him, “Go forward and kill the priests of the Lord, because they have sided with David. They knew that he was fleeing but did not tell me.” But the king's servants refused to raise their hands and sin against the priests of the Lord.

And the king said to Doeg, “You turn and strike down the priests of the Lord.” And Doeg the Syrian turned and slaughtered the priests of the Lord. On that day he killed three hundred and five men, all of whom wore the linen ephod.
He also struck Nob, the city of the priests, with the sword: men and women, children and nursing infants, cattle, donkeys, and sheep—all with the edge of the sword.
One son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to David.
And Abiathar told David that Saul had slaughtered all the priests of the Lord.
David said to Abiathar, “I knew that day that Doeg the Syrian would certainly tell Saul. I am responsible for the deaths of your father's household.
Stay with me and do not be afraid. Wherever I seek a place for myself, I will seek one for you too, so that you will be safe with me.”
David was told, “The Philistines are fighting against Keilah and have plundered the threshing floors.”
David inquired of the Lord, saying, “Shall I go and attack those Philistines?” The Lord said to David, “Go, attack the Philistines, and save Keilah.”
David's men said to him, “We are afraid even here in Judah. What will happen if we go to Keilah, where the Philistines are raiding?”
David again inquired of the Lord, and the Lord answered him and said, “Rise and go down to Keilah, for I will deliver the Philistines into your hands.”

David and the men with him went to Keilah and fought against the Philistines, who fled before him. He took their livestock and struck them with a very great slaughter. Thus David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech fled to David, he went down with David to Keilah, carrying the ephod in his hand.
Saul was told that David had come to Keilah. Saul said, “God has sold him into my hands, for he has shut himself in by entering a city with gates and bars.”
Saul ordered all the people to go down to battle at Keilah, to seize David and his men.
David knew that Saul would not cease his wickedness, and David said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod of the Lord.”
David said, “Lord, God of Israel, your servant has indeed heard that Saul intends to come against Keilah and destroy this city because of me.
Will it be besieged? Will Saul now come down here, as your servant has heard? Lord, God of Israel, tell your servant.” The Lord said, “It will be besieged.”
David said, “Will the people of Keilah deliver me and my men into Saul’s hands?” The Lord said, “They will deliver you.”
David and the men with him, about four hundred, rose and left Keilah, and went wherever they went. Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, and he stopped his expedition.

David stayed in the wilderness at Masereth, in the narrow passes. He stayed in the mountain of the wilderness of Ziph, on the gloomy mountain in the dark land. Saul sought him every day, but the Lord did not deliver him into his hands.
David saw that Saul was coming out to seek David. David was staying in the wilderness, on the gloomy mountain of Ziph, in Horesh.
Jonathan son of Saul rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hands in the Lord.
He said to him, “Do not be afraid, for the hand of Saul my father will not find you. You will reign over Israel, and I will be second to you. Saul my father knows that this is so.”
The two of them made a covenant before the Lord. David remained in Horesh, and Jonathan went to his home.
The Ziphites went up from the gloomy land to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is not David hiding among us at Masera, in the narrow passes of Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah, south of Jeshimon?
Now let the king come down to us, according to all his heart’s desire, for we will shut him into the king’s hands.”
Saul said to them, “May you be blessed by the Lord, for you have felt compassion for me.
Now go, make further preparations, observe and see the place where his feet are. Hurry there, where you say he is, lest he act cunningly.

Investigate and examine every place where he may be hiding, and return to me prepared. We will go with you, and if he is in the land, I will search him out with all the commanders of thousands of Judah.”
The Ziphites rose and went ahead of Saul. David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, toward the west, south of Jeshimon.
Saul and his men went to seek David. David was told, and he went down to the rock in the wilderness of Maon. Saul heard and pressed on after David into the wilderness of Maon.

Saul and his men went along this side of the mountain, while David and his men were on the other side of the mountain. David went in hiding to get away from Saul, while Saul and his men surrounded David and his men to seize them.
A messenger came to Saul and said, “Hurry and come here, for the Philistines have raided the land.”
Saul stopped pursuing David and went against the Philistines. For this reason that place was called the Rock of Division.
David left there and settled in the narrow passes of En-gedi.
When Saul returned from fighting the Philistines, he was told, “Look, David is in the wilderness of En-gedi.”
He took with him three thousand men chosen from all Israel and went to look for David and his men opposite Elim, where deer are hunted.
He came to the sheepfolds beside the road, where there was a cave. Saul went in to rest, while David and his men were sitting deep inside the cave.

David’s men said to him, “This is the day about which the Lord told you, ‘I will deliver your enemies into your hands, and you may do to them whatever seems good to you.’” David got up and secretly cut off the corner of Saul’s cloak.
Afterward David’s heart troubled him because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s cloak.
David said to his men, “May the Lord forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the Lord’s anointed, by laying my hands on him, for he is the Lord’s anointed.”
David persuaded his men with these words and did not allow them to rise up and kill Saul. Saul got up, left the cave, and went down to the road.
David got up after him and came out of the cave. He called after Saul, saying, “My lord the king!” Saul looked behind him, and David fell facedown on the ground and bowed before him.
David said to Saul, “Why do you listen to the words of people who say, ‘David seeks your life’?

“Today your own eyes have seen how the Lord delivered you into my hands there in the cave. I did not want to kill you, but spared you and said, ‘I will not lay my hand on my master, for he is the Lord’s anointed.’

“Look, my father! Here is the corner of your cloak in my hand. I cut off the corner of your garment but did not kill you. Know and see today that there is no evil, contempt, or wickedness in my hand, and that I have not sinned against you. Yet you hunt down my life to take it.
“May the Lord judge between me and you, and may the Lord avenge me on you, but my hand will not be against you.
“As the old proverb says, ‘Harm comes from lawless hands,’ but my hand will not be against you.
“Now, whom have you come out after, king of Israel? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A single flea?”
“May the Lord be judge and arbiter between me and you. May the Lord see and judge my case and secure justice for me against you.”
When David finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, “Is that your voice, my son David?” Saul raised his voice and wept.
Saul said to David, “You are more righteous than I am, for you have repaid me with good, while I have repaid you with evil.
“Today you have told me what good you have done to me, and how the Lord placed me in your hands today, yet you did not kill me.
“For how could someone find his enemy in distress and send him safely on his way? May the Lord repay him with good, as you have done today.
“Now I know that you will surely become king, and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands.
“Now swear to me by the Lord that you will not destroy my descendants after me or erase my name from my father’s house.”
David swore to Saul. Saul went to his own place, and David and his men came to Masara, in the narrow pass.
Samuel died, and all Israel gathered and mourned him. They buried him at his house in Ramathaim. David then set out and went down to the wilderness of Maon.
There was a man in Maon whose flocks were in Carmel. The man was very wealthy: he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. His flocks were being shorn in Carmel.
His name was Nabal, and his wife's name was Abigail. His wife had great wisdom and was very beautiful in appearance, but the man was harsh, evil in his intentions, and doglike in character.
David heard that day that Nabal the Carmelite was shearing his flocks.
David sent ten young men, and David said to the young men, “Go up to Carmel, go to Nabal, and greet him in my name.
Say this: ‘May you be well in these days, and may your household and everything you have be well.

Now, I have heard that your flocks are being shorn. They were with us here in the wilderness, and we did not hinder them or make any demands on them throughout all the days they were with us in Carmel.

Ask your young men, and they will tell you. May these young men find favor in your eyes, for they have come on a festive day. Please give whatever you have at hand to your servants and to your son David.’”
David's young men came and spoke to Nabal in David's name, repeating all these words.
He became indignant and answered David's servants, saying, “Who is David, or who is the son of Jesse? Nowadays there are many runaway servants, each fleeing from his own master.
Am I to take my bread, my wine, and the meat I slaughtered as provisions for my shearers, and give them to men whose origins I do not know?”
David's young men turned back on their way, came to David, and reported these words.

David said to his men, “Each of you, strap your sword to your waist.” Each man strapped his sword to his waist, and David also strapped his sword to his waist. About four hundred men went up after David, while two hundred remained there with the baggage.
One of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, saying, “David sent messengers from the wilderness to bless our master, but he turned away from them.
The men were very good to us. They did not hinder us or demand anything from us while we were with them out in the open country.
They were like a wall around us, by night and by day, throughout all the days we were with them tending the flocks.
Now consider and see what you should do, for disaster has been determined against our master and his entire household. He is a wicked man, and there is no speaking to him.”

Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves, two containers of wine, five prepared sheep, five measures of roasted grain flour, a measure of raisins, and two hundred fig cakes, and loaded them onto donkeys.
She said to her young men, “Go ahead of me, and I will follow you.” But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
As she mounted her donkey and went down along the sheltered side of the mountain, David and his men were coming down toward her, and she met them.

David said, “So it was in vain that I guarded everything Nabal had there in the wilderness. We did not demand to take anything at all from all that belonged to him, yet he has repaid me with evil for the good I did him.”
May God do this and more to David if by morning I leave anyone belonging to Nabal who urinates against a wall.
When Abigail saw David, she hurried down from the donkey, fell facedown before David, and bowed to him with her face to the ground.
She fell at his feet and said, “The blame is mine, my lord. But let your servant speak in your hearing, and listen to the words of your servant.
Let my lord pay no attention to this wicked man Nabal, for he is just like his name. His name is Nabal, and foolishness is with him. But I, your servant, did not see the young men you sent.

Now, as the Lord lives and as you live, since the Lord has kept you from shedding innocent blood and has made you hold back your hand, may your enemies and those who seek to harm my lord be like Nabal.
Now accept this gift that your maidservant has brought to my lord, and give it to the young men who attend my lord.
Forgive your maidservant’s offense, for the Lord will surely establish a lasting house for my lord, because the Lord fights my lord’s battles. May evil never be found in you.

No one will rise up to pursue you and seek your life. May my lord’s life be bound in the bundle of life belonging to the Lord God, and may you sling away the lives of your enemies from the hollows of slings.
When the Lord has done for my lord all the good things that he promised to bring upon you, and has appointed you by his command as ruler over Israel,

may it not be a defilement or a stumbling block in my lord’s heart that he shed innocent blood without cause. May my lord hold back his hand. When the Lord does good to my lord, remember your maidservant and do good to her.
David said to Abigail, “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today.
“Blessed be your good judgment, and blessed be you, who have kept me here today from shedding blood and have made me hold back my hand.

“But as the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, who has kept me today from harming you, if you had not hurried and come to meet me—for I had said that by morning light not one who urinates against a wall would remain to Nabal.”
David took from her hands everything she had brought him and said to her, “Go home in peace. See, I have listened to your voice and shown you favor.”
Abigail went to Nabal, and there was a feast in his house like a king’s feast. Nabal’s heart was merry within him, and he was very drunk. She told him nothing, great or small, until morning light.
And in the morning, when Nabal had sobered up from the wine, his wife told him these things. His heart died within him, and he became like a stone.
About ten days passed, and the Lord struck Nabal, and he died.

David heard that Nabal had died and said, “Blessed be the Lord God, who has judged my case concerning the insults I received from Nabal, and has delivered his servant from evil deeds. The Lord has brought Nabal’s wickedness back upon his own head.” Then David sent word to Abigail, asking to take her as his wife.
And David’s servants came to Abigail at Carmel, spoke with her, and said, “David sent us to you to take you as his wife.”
And she rose, bowed with her face to the ground, and said, “Here is your maidservant, ready to serve by washing the feet of my lord’s servants.”
Abigail hurried and arose, mounted a donkey, and five young women followed her. She went after David’s servants and became his wife.
David also took Ahinoam from Jezreel, and both women were his wives.
Saul gave his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Paltiel son of Jemessai, from Romma.
The Ziphites came out of the gloom to Saul on the hill and said, “Look, David is hiding among us on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon.”
Saul arose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph, with three thousand chosen men of Israel, to seek David in the wilderness of Ziph.
Saul camped on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon, beside the road. David was staying in the wilderness. When David saw that Saul had come after him into the wilderness,
David sent spies and learned that Saul had come fully prepared to Keilah.

And David rose secretly and came to the place where Saul was staying. David saw the place where Saul slept, and there was Abner son of Ner, his army commander. Saul was sleeping in the covered wagon, and the army was encamped around him.
David spoke to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, saying, “Who will go into the camp with me to Saul?” Abishai said, “I will go with you.”
David and Abishai entered the camp at night. There was Saul, sleeping in his covered chariot, with his spear stuck in the ground beside his head, while Abner and his troops were sleeping around him.
Abishai said to David, “The Lord has delivered your enemies into your hands today. Now let me strike him to the ground with this spear just once; I will not strike a second time.”
David said to Abishai, “Do not strike him, for who can lay his hand on the Lord’s anointed and remain innocent?”
David said, “As the Lord lives, either the Lord will punish him, or his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish.”
“May the Lord forbid that I should lay my hand on the Lord’s anointed! But now take the spear by his head and the jug of water, and let us go away.”

David took the spear and the jug of water from beside his head, and they went away. No one saw them, no one knew, and no one woke up, for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them.
David crossed to the other side and stood on top of the hill some distance away, with a great distance between them.
David called out to the army and spoke to Abner, saying, “Will you not answer, Abner?” He said, “Who are you, calling to me in the king’s presence?”
David said to Abner, “Are you not a brave man? Who is like you in Israel? Why, then, do you not guard your lord the king? For someone came into your army to kill your lord the king.”

“What you have done is not good. As the Lord lives, you deserve death, you who guard your lord the king, the Lord’s anointed. And now, look: where are the king’s spear and the jug of water that were beside his head?”
Saul recognized David’s voice and said, “Is that your voice, my son David?” David said, “I am your servant, my lord the king.”
He said, “Why is this, my lord, that you are pursuing your servant? What sin have I committed, and what wrongdoing has been found in me?”

“And now, let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If God has stirred you up against me, may your sacrifice give off a pleasing aroma. But if it is human beings, may they be cursed before the Lord, because today they have driven me away from having a place in the Lord’s inheritance, saying, ‘Go, serve foreign gods.’”
“Now may my blood not fall to the ground before the Lord, for the king of Israel has come out to seek my life, as one would chase a raven through the mountains.”
And Saul said, “I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will do you no harm, because my life is precious in your eyes. Today I have been foolish and very guilty.”
David answered and said, “Here is the king’s spear. Let one of your young men come across and take it.”
“May the Lord repay everyone according to their righteousness and faithfulness, for the Lord delivered you into my hands today, but I was unwilling to lay my hand on the Lord’s anointed.”
“Just as your life was precious in my eyes here today, so may my life be precious before the Lord. May he strengthen me and deliver me from every distress.”
Saul said to David, “Blessed are you, my son David! You will surely accomplish much and surely grow strong.” David went on his way, and Saul returned to his own place.

David spoke in his heart and said, “Now I will fall into Saul’s hands one day. There is nothing better for me than to go away to the land of the Philistines. Even if Saul searches for me throughout all the territory of Israel, I will escape from his hands.”
David arose and crossed over, he and the six hundred men who were with him, and went to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
David lived with Achish in Gath, he and his men, each with his household, and David with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel.
Saul was told that David had fled to Gath, and he no longer searched for him.

David said to Achish, “If your servant has found favor in your eyes, give me a place in one of the towns in the countryside, and I will live there. Why should your servant live with you in the royal city?”
That day Achish gave him Ziklag. Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.
The length of time David lived in the country of the foreigners was four months.
David and the men with him went out and raided all the Geshurites, Gezerites, and Amalekites. The land was inhabited from Gelamsur, from the secure fortified settlements, as far as Egypt.
David struck the land and left neither man nor woman alive. He took flocks, herds, donkeys, camels, and clothing, then returned and came to Achish.
Achish said to David, “Which region did you raid today?” David said to Achish, “The southern regions of Judah, the regions of Jerahmeel, and the regions of Kenaz.”

“I left neither man nor woman alive to be brought to Gath, for I say, ‘News about us might reach Gath, and they might say, “This is what David does.”’” This was his practice throughout all the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines.
Achish trusted David completely and said, “He is utterly disgraced among his own people, Israel, and he will be my servant forever.”
In those days the Philistines gathered their armies to go out and fight against Israel. Achish said to David, “Know for certain that you and your men will go out with me to battle.”
David said to Achish, “So be it. Now you will know what your servant will do.” Achish said to David, “So be it. I will make you commander of my bodyguard for all time.”
Samuel died, and all Israel mourned him and buried him in his own city, Ramathaim. Saul had removed the mediums and diviners from the land.
The Philistines assembled, came, and camped at Shunem. Saul gathered all the men of Israel, and they camped at Gilboa.
When Saul saw the Philistine army, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
Saul inquired of the Lord, but the Lord did not answer him through dreams, divination, or prophets.
Saul said to his servants, “Find me a woman who is a medium, so that I may go to her and inquire through her.” His servants said to him, “There is a woman who is a medium at Endor.”

Saul disguised himself, put on different clothes, and went with two men. They came to the woman at night. He said to her, “Divine for me through your necromancy, and bring up for me the one I name to you.”
The woman said, “You yourself know what Saul has done, how he has destroyed the mediums and diviners from the land. Why, then, are you laying a trap for my life, to kill me?”
Saul swore to her by the Lord and said, “As the Lord lives, no harm will come to you because of this matter.”
The woman said, “Whom shall I bring up for you?” He said, “Bring up Samuel for me.”
And the woman saw Samuel and cried out with a loud voice. The woman said to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!”
The king said to her, “Do not be afraid. Tell me whom you saw.” The woman said to him, “I see gods coming up from the earth.”

He said to her, “What did you perceive?” She said to him, “A man coming up from the earth, standing upright, with a cloak wrapped around him.” Saul recognized that it was Samuel, fell facedown to the ground, and bowed before him.

Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?” Saul said, “I am in great distress. The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has departed from me and has not answered me, either through prophets or through dreams. So I have called you to show me what I should do.”
Samuel said, “Why do you question me, when the Lord has departed from you and sided with your neighbor?
The Lord has done to you what he spoke through me. The Lord will tear the kingdom from your hands and give it to your neighbor, David.
Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord and did not carry out his fierce anger against Amalek, the Lord has done this to you today.

The Lord will deliver Israel, together with you, into the hands of the Philistines. Tomorrow you will fall, and your sons will fall with you. The Lord will also give the army of Israel into the hands of the Philistines.”
Saul immediately fell full length to the ground and was greatly terrified by Samuel’s words. He had no strength left in him, because he had eaten no food all that day and all that night.
The woman came to Saul and saw that he was deeply distressed. She said to him, “Look, your servant has listened to your voice. I took my life in my hands and obeyed the words you spoke to me.
Now you too must listen to your servant’s voice. Let me set a piece of bread before you, and eat, so that you may have strength to go on your way.”
And he would not eat, but his servants and the woman urged him, and he listened to them. He rose from the ground and sat on a seat.
The woman had a fattened calf in the house, and she hurried and slaughtered it. She took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread.
And she set it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they rose and left that night.
The Philistines gathered all their armies at Aphek, and Israel camped at Endor in Jezreel.
The Philistine commanders marched with their hundreds and thousands, and David and his men marched at the rear with Achish.

The Philistine commanders said, “Who are these men passing by?” Achish said to the Philistine commanders, “Is this not David, the servant of Saul, king of Israel? He has been with us for two years, and I have found no fault in him from the day he came over to us until today.”

The Philistine commanders became angry with him and said to him, “Send the man back. Let him go to the place where you stationed him. He must not come with us into battle, or he may betray our army. How could he regain his master’s favor except with the heads of these men?
Is this not David, about whom they sang as they danced, saying, ‘Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”

Achish called David and said to him, “As the Lord lives, you are upright and good in my eyes, and so are your coming and going with me here in the camp. I have found no evil in you from the day you came to me until this very day. But the commanders do not look favorably on you.
So now turn back and go in peace, and do nothing displeasing in the eyes of the Philistine commanders.”

David said to Achish, “What have I done to you? What have you found in your servant from the day I came before you until today, that I should not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?”
Achish answered David, “I know that you are pleasing in my eyes, like an angel of God. But the Philistine commanders say, ‘He must not come with us into battle.’

Now rise early in the morning, you and your master’s servants who have come with you, and go to the place where I stationed you. Do not harbor any ill feeling in your heart, for you are pleasing to me. Rise early for your journey, and when it is light, depart.”
David and his men rose early to leave in the morning and guard the land of the Philistines. The Philistines went up to fight against Israel.
When David and his men entered Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had raided the southern region and Ziklag. They had attacked Ziklag and burned it with fire.
And he took captive the women and everything in it, from small to great. They killed neither man nor woman, but took them captive and went on their way.
David and his men came to the city, and there was the city burned down, with their wives, sons, and daughters taken captive.
David and his men raised their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep.
Both of David’s wives had been taken captive: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel.
David was greatly distressed, because the people spoke of stoning him. All the people were bitter in spirit, each over his own sons and daughters. But David found strength in the Lord his God.
David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Bring the ephod.” Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
David asked the Lord, saying, “Shall I pursue that raiding party? Will I overtake them?” The Lord said to him, “Pursue them. You will certainly overtake them and certainly rescue the captives.”
David went with the four hundred men who were with him. They came to the Besor ravine, and the remaining men stayed there.
David pursued with four hundred men, while two hundred men remained, staying on the other side of the Besor ravine.
They found an Egyptian man in the countryside, took hold of him, and brought him to David in the countryside. They gave him bread, and he ate, and they gave him water to drink.
And they gave him a piece of a fig cake and two raisin cakes. He ate, and his spirit was strengthened by this, for he had eaten no bread and drunk no water for three days and three nights.

And David said to him, “Whose servant are you, and where are you from?” The young man said, “I am an Egyptian, the servant of an Amalekite man. My master abandoned me because I fell ill three days ago.”
“We raided the southern regions of the Cherethites, the regions of Judea, and the southern region of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire.”

David said to him, “Will you lead me down to that raiding party?” The Egyptian said to him, “Swear to me that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master, and I will lead you down to the raiding party.” And he swore to him.

He led him down there, and there they were, scattered over the face of the whole land, eating, drinking, and celebrating with all the great spoil they had taken from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah.
David came upon them and struck them down from the rising of the morning star until evening and into the next day. Not one of them escaped except four hundred young men who mounted camels and fled.
David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives.
Nothing of theirs was missing, from the smallest to the greatest, neither sons nor daughters nor spoil nor anything they had taken from them. David brought everything back.
And David took all the flocks and herds and drove them ahead of the spoil. He gave the spoil this name: “This is David’s spoil.”

David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow him and whom he had made stay at the Besor ravine. They came out to meet David and the force with him. David approached the men and asked after their well-being, greeting them in peace.

All the wicked and worthless men among the warriors who had gone with David answered him, saying, “Since they did not join us in the pursuit, we will not give them any of this spoil we recovered. Let each take only his wife and children and go away.”
David said, “Let it not be so, my brothers, after the Lord has given them to us and protected us. The Lord delivered into our hands the raiding party that came against us.

“Who will listen to these words of yours? They are in no way inferior to you. The share of the one who guards the baggage shall be the same as the share of the one who goes into battle. They shall receive equal shares.”
From that day onward, this became a law and an ordinance in Israel, continuing to this day.
David came to Ziklag and sent some of the spoil to the elders of Judah and to his friends, saying, “Here is a gift for you from the spoil of the Lord’s enemies.”
To you who are in Bethel and in Ramoth of the south,
And those in Jattir and Aroer, and those in Siphmoth, and those in Eshtemoa.
and to those in Erakel, those in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, and those in the cities of the Kenites,
those in Hormah, those in Chorashan, and those in Athach,
and those in Hebron and in all the places through which David himself and his men had traveled.
The Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell wounded on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua, Saul’s sons.
The battle grew fierce around Saul. Strong men armed with bows found him, and he was wounded beneath the ribs.

Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and pierce me with it, lest these uncircumcised men come and stab me and mock me.” But his armor-bearer refused, because he was very afraid. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it.
When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his own sword and died with him.
So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that day.

When the Israelites who were beyond the valleys and beyond the Jordan saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their towns and fled. The Philistines came up and settled in them.
The next day, the Philistines came to strip the dead and found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.
They turned him over, stripped off his clothing, and cut off his head. They sent heralds throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news to their idols and to the people.
They placed his equipment in the temple of Astarte and hung their bodies on the wall of Beth-shan.
The inhabitants of Jabesh in Gilead heard about them—what the Philistines had done to Saul.
And all the valiant men rose and traveled all night. They took Saul’s body and the body of his son Jonathan from the wall of Beth-shan, brought them to Jabesh, and burned them there.
They took their bones and buried them beneath the field at Jabesh, and they fasted for seven days.
